title: Invoice Export
tagline: Bookkeepers get every invoice out of Fieldnote in one click, in their tool's format.

round.title: PDF bundles and the monthly send

problem.statement: Every month our customers' bookkeepers copy invoices out of Fieldnote by hand. They rebuild a spreadsheet, download PDFs one at a time, and email them on. It takes hours and the totals often drift.
today: 41 support tickets in September asked for an export
PDFs download one at a time, about 4 seconds each
Nobody can see who took which invoices out

quotes.text: I spend the first Monday of every month copying numbers between two tabs.
Make it one button. My bookkeeper should never need to log in.

outcomes.claim: Anyone with the finance role downloads a zip of PDFs for any date range, 2,000 invoices in under 30 seconds.
done_when: 2,000 invoices zip in under 30 seconds on staging

outcomes.claim: Every export is recorded with who ran it, when, and which invoices left.

findings.finding: Bookkeepers rebuild the spreadsheet by hand every month.
findings.solution: One CSV with presets for the three tools our customers use most.

findings.finding: PDFs render on the web server, about 4 seconds each, one at a time.
findings.solution: Render in a background worker, 8 at a time, and cache each PDF by invoice version.
findings.detail: The web server renders each PDF inside the request that asked for it. A month of 300 invoices takes about 20 minutes and times out after 60 seconds, so bookkeepers download them one by one.
findings.solution_detail: A worker pulls render jobs from the queue, eight at a time, and stores each PDF keyed by invoice version. A second export of the same month reuses the stored files and only renders what changed.

findings.finding: There is no record of who downloaded which invoices.
findings.solution: Every export writes one row: who, when, filters and invoice count.

findings.finding: Date filters use UTC, so month ends drift for customers in the Americas.
findings.solution: Filter by the account's own time zone everywhere exports run.

research.question: What CSV layout do the accounting tools our customers use actually import?
research.answer: All three accept one row per invoice with a fixed set of columns. Two of them also accept one row per line item, which bookkeepers prefer for tax splits.
recommendations: Ship one row per invoice as the default
Offer line items as a preset, not a setting

research.question: How do we render 2,000 PDFs in under 30 seconds?
research.answer: A worker pool of 8 renders about 90 PDFs a second once warm. Caching by invoice version removes most of the work for repeat exports.
recommendations: Move rendering to a queue worker
Cache PDFs by invoice id and version

research.question: Do bookkeepers want the monthly export by email or in a shared folder?
research.answer: Email, by a wide margin. They forward it into their own systems and do not want another login.
recommendations: Email a link that expires after 7 days

architecture.summary: Exports run as background jobs so the web app stays fast. Each job writes a record, renders what it needs, and hands the file to storage or email.

areas.title: Exports run as background jobs
areas.short: Take the slow work off the web server
areas.found: Every export runs inside a web request. Under load the request times out after 60 seconds, and nothing records what was exported, by whom, or with which filters.
areas.recommend: The web app only queues a job and returns at once. A job runner does the work, writes one history row per run, and tells the screen when the file is ready.
areas.why: It is the standard pattern for slow work in web apps, our framework ships a job queue already, and it gives the audit record for free.
areas.user_sees: The export button answers at once, a progress chip shows the job, and a history page lists every past export.
tradeoffs: One more process to run and watch
A finished export arrives a few seconds later than a tiny one does today
not_building: A custom queue; we use the framework's

areas.title: A worker renders PDFs in parallel
areas.short: From 20 minutes to about 2 for a month
areas.found: PDFs render one at a time on the web server, about 4 seconds each, so a month of 300 invoices takes 20 minutes.
areas.recommend: A separate worker renders eight PDFs at a time and stores each one by invoice version, then zips the month.
areas.why: Rendering is the slow step and it is independent per invoice, so parallel workers cut the time almost linearly; caching by version avoids repeat work.
areas.user_sees: A month of PDFs arrives as one zip in about two minutes.

steps.text: The job splits the month into one render task per invoice.

plan.summary: We build exports as background jobs in four waves of parallel agents. CSV and the job runner come first, then PDF bundles, then the monthly send. Every ticket proves itself with a test and a screenshot before the gate.

where_found: apps/web/src/invoices/render.ts:88, export runs in the request
reproduce: Open the invoice list with 300 invoices in one month
The request times out after 60 seconds and no history exists
tickets.solution: Queue each export as a background job using the framework's job queue. The runner retries twice, writes one history row per run, and posts progress the screen can poll.
tickets.why_right: The framework already ships the queue, so this adds no new service and gives the audit record in the same change.
